summary:
Khakassia, a republic within the Russian Federation, stands under Russia's national legal framework, and the source record shows no sub-national variation in how that framework is applied. The law signed by President Putin in 2023 prohibits gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents, which means neither visitors nor residents of Khakassia can obtain recognised legal gender status, and trans-specific healthcare has been effectively banned since the same year. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, and no statutory discrimination protection exists on grounds of gender identity.

The expanded federal propaganda law criminalises any public expression, explicitly including anything that 'justifies' gender transition. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, advises against all travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers; it states that foreigners found guilty of violating the propaganda law may be detained for up to 15 days and deported, and that displaying rainbow symbols is a crime. The Russian government separately issues its own warnings telling LGBT travellers they face these consequences. These are country-wide federal rules with no sub-national variation.

Following the Supreme Court's designation of the 'international LGBT movement' as an extremist organisation, Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions by 30 June 2025 for alleged participation in that movement or for displaying its alleged symbols, comprising 98 administrative and 3 criminal convictions. At least 20 people faced criminal charges from January 2024 onward, and three publishing-house staff charged on 15 May 2025 face up to 12 years in prison. Repeated display of banned symbols carries up to four years in prison.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) applies the refugee convention standard to Russia and finds that LGB people are not generally at real risk of persecution solely for their sexual orientation, while trans people, public LGBT+ advocates and people in the North Caucasus are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. The same note records no division-specific facts for Khakassia.

Enforcement has been swift and physical. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. Cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in two years. In December 2024 a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.
tangentialFactors:
The risk assessment for a trans visitor diverges sharply from the assessment for a lesbian or gay visitor under the same framework. The UK Home Office note treats sexual orientation and gender identity separately: general risk is not established for LGB people as a whole, but trans people and public LGBT+ advocates are identified as likely to face persecution, which places a trans traveller in a different evidentiary category at any asylum interview.

The scale of the national regime is documented. The UK Home Office note counts 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across Russia between 2022 and 2024, and Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing the country. Meduza reported that propaganda-law cases have grown eighteenfold over the past decade.

Community life has been driven underground by raids and extremism charges. The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life through 2025, quoting a St Petersburg queer woman who described herself as a second-class citizen after the extremist designation. A trans woman interviewed by BBC Russian on 27 July 2024 described being held for nine months at a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk after being lured there by relatives in summer 2021, where she was forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping.
localsOnly:
Residents of Khakassia cannot change their legal gender on Russian documents, cannot access gender-affirming healthcare through legal channels, and have no statutory discrimination recourse. Residents convicted under the extremism provisions face the same administrative and criminal exposure recorded nationally: 98 administrative convictions and 3 criminal convictions by 30 June 2025, with criminal charges carrying sentences of up to four years for repeat display of banned symbols and up to 12 years in the publishing-house case of 15 May 2025.

Publication, printing and distribution work carries particular exposure, since the three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 were prosecuted for material treated as extremist. Fines under the propaganda statutes function as a revenue source for the state budget rather than an incidental sanction.

Assessment for residents mirrors the assessment for visitors: the UK Home Office treats trans people and public LGBT+ advocates in Russia as a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the standard for UK asylum claims, while finding that LGB people are not generally at real risk solely for their sexual orientation.
outOfScopeNotes:
No division-specific facts for Khakassia appear in any of the three sources. Whether local authorities in the Khakassia interior carry out bar raids, extremism prosecutions or conversion-practice cases is not sourced in this inventory, and no regional divergence from the national pattern is recorded either way.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note cited here is version 2.0, June 2025, with its page updated 12 August 2026; whether that update altered the assessment of trans people is not resolved by the inventory.

The count of 101 extremism-related convictions is stated as of 30 June 2025 and will have moved since; the inventory carries no later figure. The breakdown of the 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 by category of law or by region is not itemised in the sources.
